answer: The applicant books one reed-cutter's hide on a charted lagoon and mills a brass cipher rotor punched through the hide's deed plate. At an unannounced dawn the warden records the sparrow roost in the eaves; within minutes the rotor must be set to that spectrogram hash and closed under a one-shot lead seal. Inspectors break the seal and match rotor cuts, plate punch, and official tape. Shared hides, reused rotors, or pre-dawn seals are slashed as one farm. Fielding N identities costs N lagoon hides, N uniquely milled rotors, and N dawn sittings no single listener can cover in the same hour.
